turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Monday, the nineteenth of October. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
[curious] Three up top. Iran has put a number of days on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and the number is seven.
[wry] A sanctions law was waived the day before it was due to start working.
[deadpan] And Apple sold out a folding phone in half an hour that you will hold in late January.
There's a thread there. Start with the strait.
Saturday the seventeenth. Baghdad. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, at the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
What did he actually offer?
Seven days. The strait reopens on the sixth day, talks begin on the seventh. His words: the choice now rests with the United States.
[curious] And Washington said?
Nothing. No American official has answered on the record. It's an offer with a condition attached, which is not the same as a date.
[thoughtful] Okay. Meanwhile the Revolutionary Guard is saying something different.
Entirely. On the seventeenth they said a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels struck a mine and exploded.
Which tanker?
[pause] That's the point. No vessel name. No flag. No owner. No cargo origin. And no maritime authority has confirmed it. As a claim, by one party, and we say so.
What about the counting? Last week the body that counts attacks said it couldn't count them.
This week it has a figure. At least ten vessels attacked in the week to the eighteenth. Twenty-three since the first of October. A weekly high for the war.
[curious] And yet — you told me before we came in that the strait is getting busier?

Lloyd's List Intelligence counted at least four hundred and seventy-seven transits in September. The busiest month since the war began in late February. Bulk carriers crossed fifty-nine times against a spring average of twenty-four.
[laughs] So which is it? Closed or record traffic?

Both, and that's the honest answer. The strait didn't shut. It got expensive. Freight is now twenty-five to thirty per cent of the cost of Gulf crude. Before the war it was one to three. And the oil comes out a different door. Ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Kutch, off India's west coast, hit eighty-two in September.
So the cargo still moves, it just moves sideways and costs a fortune.
Brent passed a hundred and ten dollars on Friday in New York. Settled at a hundred and nine point eight six.
Is anyone arguing with Tehran's position?

Hamidreza Azizi of the International Crisis Group. His line: the question is whether Tehran is overestimating its ability to sustain this pressure. Friday the seventeenth. The President signed an order waiving every Russian provision of the Graham Act. The provisions were due to take effect on the eighteenth. Tariffs of up to five hundred per cent on Russian goods. Up to one hundred per cent on the five largest buyers of Russian crude and gas. Bank sanctions. The sovereign debt ban.
All of it?
That's where our two sources disagree, and we print the disagreement rather than resolve it.
Good. Who's angry?
Republicans, mostly. Thom Tillis of North Carolina called it beyond irresponsible. John Cornyn of Texas said Graham himself would be appalled.
And Kyiv?
Zelensky: the decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me.
What did America get for it?
[pause] As of Friday, no Russian diesel had been identified reaching the world market.
So the thing given up is real and the thing bought for it hasn't arrived.

Correct. And a correction we owe you: we said on Sunday the waiver came on the sixteenth with no expiry. It was the seventeenth, it's revocable, and the Act's Russian provisions sunset in twenty thirty-one. Polls close at eight in the evening Mountain Time. That's ten o'clock tomorrow morning here. [deadpan] They're voting on ten questions.
Ten?

Five on immigration and provincial services. Four proposing constitutional amendments. And a tenth one. Sort of. It asks whether the government should begin the legal process toward a future binding referendum on separation.
[laughs] A vote about whether to start deciding whether to have a vote. Does the polling tell us anything?

Seventy per cent to remain, twenty-two to begin the process, seven undecided. That's Leger, a thousand and one Albertans, the second to fourth of October. Saturday we printed sixty-six to thirty-four. No poll we read produces that. Our error. Section one, subsection four of Canada's Clarity Act. A clear expression of will can't come from a question that merely seeks a mandate to negotiate. Arguably exactly that. A yes may buy less than either side is campaigning for.
Okay. Money and home. Singapore first — the haze.

It broke overnight. The environment agency's own feed at five this morning read ninety-three in the north. First time this episode. West is still a hundred and forty-one. But Sunday morning the west hit two hundred and thirty.
So it's over?
It's a wind event, not an enforcement one. The agency warns smoke may come back from Tuesday night.
And the law? Seven Indonesian companies were named on Friday.
[deadpan] Three of the seven got materially identical notices in two thousand and fifteen. Eleven years, two sets of notices, the same three companies.
What can the Act actually do?
Up to a hundred thousand Singapore dollars for each day haze occurs here. Another fifty thousand a day for ignoring a notice.
And how much has ever been collected?
Nothing. And there's no deadline attached to the notices anywhere we could read.
[sighs] Is anyone defending it?

Two academics put the real problem plainly. Jolene Lin at the National University notes the twenty-fifteen use drew Indonesian complaints about sovereignty. Michelle Lim at the Management University points out Singapore's access to the corporate information depends on what Jakarta allows.
And the minister?
Grace Fu says enforcement will not be easy, but Singapore must try. Note the tense.
What's life actually like?

A hardware forum thread this week is entirely about whether a surgical mask is any use. One poster: no use, need N ninety-five. Another: wearing one is the same as don't wear. N ninety-fives sold out in many pharmacies. People are ordering KF ninety-fours from Pinduoduo. One man took his filtration advice from a chatbot. Nobody in that thread mentions the agency, the law or Indonesia at all.
Markets. What happened?

[curious] Thursday the fifteenth is the day to understand. Producer prices came in up one point three per cent on the month. Six point three on the year. Very hot. And the price of thirty-year American government money went down.
[gasps] Down? On a six per cent print?
The ten-year fell nine basis points that day. Closed the week at five point zero nine.
Explain that to me like I've just walked in.

The Fed raised in September, to three and three-quarters to four per cent. Then on the thirteenth John Williams capped the terminal rate — one more hike this year, none expected next. And once the top is in sight, an oil shock stops being an inflation story and becomes a demand-destruction story. A tax on growth, not a signal of prices.
So the bond market looked at a hundred and ten dollar oil and bought the long bond.
Exactly that. And the curve has changed direction — two-year to ten-year has flattened from plus forty-four to plus thirty-five basis points.
Which is the opposite of what we said a week ago.
It is, and we say so on the page.
Who called it wrong?

[wry] This is the nice bit. Ian Lyngen at BMO wrote on the eighth that the market remains content to trade the energy shock solely from the perspective of the inflationary implications. Eight days later the market did precisely the opposite.
What about Singapore's own policy?
The Monetary Authority held its band on the fourteenth. Third-quarter growth at five point four per cent, core inflation back at two point one.
And gold? Bitcoin?

Gold is the odd one out. Real yields fell, which normally lifts it, and it fell anyway — about eight-tenths of a per cent. Bitcoin read the liquidity side badly: eighty-six thousand five hundred on the fifth of October, eighty-two thousand on the sixteenth. Market explanation. Never advice. China's commerce and science ministries published a draft export-control list on Friday. Forty technologies, twenty-three of them in artificial intelligence.
What's the threshold?
Weights, source code and core components of any model at or above two trillion parameters — or in the global top ten on performance and safety tests.
Does that kill open-weight models out of China?
[thoughtful] Not quite, and the detail is the story. There's still an open-source route. But it's an automatic licence conditional on reporting in advance — and the licence can be revoked.
So an exemption became a permission slip. [amused] And how do we know this?

Because a reader on Hacker News wanted to check what the draft actually said, found it published in proprietary Chinese office software, and installed the software to read it. And having read it, he found the deepfake-detection thresholds apparently printed backwards. Banned above ninety-five per cent accuracy, merely restricted above ninety-eight.
[chuckles] So the draft needs work. The home lab. What can I actually run this week?

[amused] A twenty-seven-billion-parameter model on a PlayStation five. A developer released a build of llama dot c p p for a jailbroken console. It serves models over your home network with a browser chat page and a television interface.
How fast?
Eleven point four gigabytes of shared memory available. A small model at two hundred and seven tokens a second. The twenty-seven billion, squeezed to two bits, at about twenty.
And people believe the numbers?
They're the author's own, but one commenter independently reports the same twenty. Three hundred and seventy-two points, eighty-five comments in two days.
What's the catch?
Two bits is two bits. One reader calls it entirely useless given the limited memory. Another says it won't replace a frontier model for most people.
[warmly] But it's a two-hundred-dollar machine doing two-hundred-dollar work.

Well, and doing it on a games console somebody had already paid for. About seventy cents a day in electricity, by one commenter's own arithmetic. Apple opened pre-orders at eight o'clock Friday evening here. Two hundred and fifty-six gigabytes, three thousand and ninety-nine Singapore dollars.
Read on Apple's own store?

Our own reading of their Singapore page. Up to four thousand eight hundred and ninety-nine for two terabytes. Limit two per customer. Inside thirty minutes, with delivery estimates sliding to around the twenty-fifth of January.
[scoffs] Why open in so many places at once?
Seventy-plus countries, when the plan had been the United States and China. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman: Apple made a major mistake here.
What's the thing people aren't saying?

The seventy-nine-dollar case attaches with adhesive. And replacing the folding screen reportedly costs about what a new iPhone does. The Atelier is on exactly that theme today. Padlocks and door cylinders.
Take my hand. Actually no — that comes later. Give me the lock thing first.
[wry] ASSA ABLOY bought Sargent and Greenleaf in December. The safe-lock maker. A hundred employees, four hundred and thirty million Swedish crowns.
Who else do they own?

Their own brand directory header says twelve of a hundred and seventy-four. Another page on the same website says more than two hundred and fifty. So we print both. And the buyer's point is that a Yale and an Abloy are the same company and not remotely the same object.
How do I judge a lock without knowing the brands?
Two things. First, the step that changes the attack isn't the metal, it's open shackle to closed shackle — the body extended up around the shackle so no bolt cropper can get a bite.
And second?
The second digit of the European standard on the box. Grade four is twenty-five thousand cycles. Grade six is a hundred thousand. At four turns a day, seventeen years against sixty-eight.
[gasps] That's the whole buy-once case in one digit.

And a sceptic, from Seattle's police: the commonest forced entry is a kick, and the weakest point is almost always the strike plate. Swap the strike-plate screws for four-inch ones into the stud. Their words: this one step alone will deter or prevent most through-the-door forced entries.
[amused] A box of screws beats a five-hundred-pound padlock.
One picker put it better. A premium padlock on weak furniture is an ANSI Grade one deadbolt on a screen door.
[laughs] Right. Take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one. Koi. Nishikigoi. Japanese ornamental carp.
[curious] Fish. Okay. Sell it to me.
It isn't fishkeeping with a bigger tank. It's water engineering with a fish as the output.
Meaning?
The fish grows to its water. A dealer's first-year koi already run thirty-two to fifty-two centimetres. A two-year-old of one famous bloodline often measures seventy to seventy-five.
And they live how long?
Thirty to forty years, per Japan's own transport ministry.
So what's the catch?
[pause] The cull. The same ministry document says that of roughly two hundred thousand carp spawned, five hundred to a thousand reach adulthood.
[gasps] Five hundred out of two hundred thousand?
Ninety-nine point seven per cent. Every fish in every dealer's tank is the survivor of that.
That's the government saying it, not a campaigner. How big is this trade?
Japan exported nine point nine seven billion yen of koi last year. Up thirty-seven point nine per cent.
Who's buying?
America first. But China's imports rose seven hundred and twenty-four point six per cent in a single year.
[gasps] Seven hundred per cent?

And here's the bit that made me laugh. Work the value per kilo. America pays about forty-five thousand yen. China, forty-two thousand. Britain, fifteen thousand six hundred. Britain buys tonnage. America and China buy quality.
What's the most expensive fish ever?
A hundred-and-one-centimetre Kohaku called S Legend. Two hundred and three million yen, in twenty eighteen.
Has that been beaten?
No. Eight years, and it still stands. Though the coverage contradicts itself about whether the buyer was in Japan or Taiwan, and nobody gives a date or an auction.
Now tell me the strange one. You said there was a strange one.
[amused] Azukari. You buy a fish and you don't receive it.
Say that again?
The koi stays in Japan, in the breeder's mud pond, growing. You collect it a season or two later, larger.
What does that cost?
One Californian dealer's current list runs from three thousand dollars to twenty-six thousand — that one boarding in Dainichi's own mud pond.
And the boarding fee?
[pause] Never itemised. Folded into the purchase. No dealer we could read publishes a per-season rate. That's exactly the line we ran.
Is this a good week for it?
Perfect week. Dainichi opens the season's first on-site auction in Niigata on the twenty-fifth. Its ninety-ninth.
Can I bid?

No. Only members of the promotion association. The farm deals with the trade alone. And here's the contrast that runs the desk. While Japan's trade bodies are running their ninety-ninth auction and their sixty-second international show — The Associated Koi Clubs of America's web domain now redirects to a for-sale page. KOI USA magazine's serves a hosting placeholder. The British society's won't load at all. The community didn't collapse. It moved — to Japan's trade bodies, to dealer personalities, and to China.
Can you keep koi in Singapore?
You can trade them. An academic survey is blunt: most Singaporean farmers act as dealers. They import, grow on, and sell. They don't breed.
Why not?
The breeding and dealer licences are separate and costly. And the climate genuinely works against you — a koi here never gets the winter rest that structures the Japanese growth year.
[curious] And the famous local name? The big aquarium company?
The words koi and nishikigoi appear nowhere on Qian Hu's corporate site.
[laughs] Brilliant. What does it cost to run?
A chiller is nine hundred and sixty to one thousand four hundred and forty dollars a year. Two to six times the pump.
So the real cost here is fighting the weather.

Singapore is a great ornamental-fish trading hub and a mediocre place to grow a champion. The Lancet published a three-paper series on children's digital media. Four of the six authors on the second paper are at the National University here.
Headline number?
Two point eight million healthy years of life lost to depression. But it's a model, and the authors say the causal basis remains uncertain.
And the critics?

Alan Woodward at Surrey: calling for precautionary action is a legitimate position, but it is a value judgement, not a scientific finding. He also counted the quality ratings. Seventy-one per cent of the hundred and twenty-one underlying reviews were rated low or critically low.
What about sleep? You had something on sleep.
California moved its school start times. Teenagers there woke forty minutes later and slept thirty-eight minutes longer.
Did they just stay up later?
[deadpan] No. Bedtimes didn't move at all. And the age gradient underneath is the warning. Every year older brings a later bedtime and shorter sleep.
Fitness?

Four ageing cohorts, fifty-four thousand people, from age fifty. Exercise and cognitive-social engagement together buy twenty-four point seven years free of cognitive impairment. Neither buys seventeen and a half. [wry] No. High exercise against high social engagement — the hazard ratio between them is one point zero one. The gym does not buy you out of needing company. And company does not buy you out of needing the gym. No device measures the second half.
One for the diary before we close?
Kenshi Yonezu. One Singapore night, the twenty-ninth of January. General sale Thursday at noon.
And the film?
A twenty-four's Elizabeth Holmes documentary opened at ninety-nine on Metascore, from thirty-seven critics, none negative. Fifteen million dollars from eight hundred and fifty-five screens.
Against Street Fighter's thirty-one million from three and a half thousand.
Twice the take per screen, for a documentary of two hours fifty-four. Bangladesh. The word is hundi.
Which is?
[thoughtful] The informal transfer system. A worker in Riyadh hands cash to an agent. The agent's partner in Sylhet pays the family in taka. Nothing crosses a border except a message.
And what's the story?

Bangladesh has just posted record remittances. Thirty-five point six billion dollars in the year to June. Up seventeen point three per cent. It is read as good news everywhere. And it is measuring something else. Hundi is a two-sided market. The migrant supplies dollars abroad. But somebody inside Bangladesh has to want dollars outside it, or the agent can't square his book.
Who wants that?
Importers under-invoicing. And above all the politically connected, moving capital out.
[pause] And in August twenty twenty-four the government fell.

The demand side collapsed. The kerb premium vanished. Migrant flows didn't grow — they merely became visible. A negative image of capital flight. A monthly published measure of how little is being stolen.
[exhales] That's the most precise price anyone has put on a change of government.
And it was published in a spreadsheet, with no commentary.
Is there a precedent?

Pakistan after the eleventh of September, two thousand and one. Enforcement shut the hawala corridors. Recorded remittances went from about a billion dollars in two thousand to three and a half billion in two thousand and two.
With no change in the number of migrants.
None. Nobody started working harder. The money changed lane.
And now?
The dial is moving back. In August the money changers capped the cash dollar after the kerb hit a hundred and twenty-eight taka, against a bank rate of a hundred and twenty-two point three.
A gap of about four and a half per cent.
Which is hundi's entire margin, and it had been close to nothing. Reserves back above thirty-six billion, the fund programme eased — all of it resting on a political variable, not a productive one.
Is there a fair objection?

Two, and we concede both. The exchange-rate reform closed the gap mechanically. And part of the record is service-export income misbooked, plus currency round-tripped to harvest a two and a half per cent subsidy.
Does conceding them hurt the argument?

[thoughtful] It sharpens it. If the state's own flagship number can't tell a migrant's wages from a round-trip, then a country whose external position depends on that number hasn't stabilised. And it wrote the luck down as income.
[pause] That's the whole issue, isn't it. Dates and numbers that look like commitments.
Seven days if Washington agrees. A law waived before it worked. A vote about whether to vote. Notices with no deadline.
A phone you pay for in October and hold in January.
And ten grams of a Martian moon, in twenty thirty-one.
[warmly] Against all that, one thing on the cover keeps its appointment.
A mainspring one point eight metres long, coiled into a steel case, that runs for exactly ten days and then stops.
[chuckles] The difference between a promise and a specification.
Somebody measured the second one.
[exhales] That's the Briefing, then.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
